Curves & concepts 11

Load-deflection curve Fig 9.2

Stiffness = the slope · range = how far it reaches · springback = elastic recovery.

Stress-strain curve Fig 9.3

A material property, independent of wire geometry; its slope is the modulus E.

Resilience & formability Fig 9.4

Resilience = area under the curve to yield; formability = how far it bends before it breaks.

Superelasticity Fig 9.5

A stress-induced austenite → martensite transformation.

A-NiTi force plateau Fig 9.6

The flat plateau delivers a near-constant force across a long range — ideal for alignment.

Hysteresis Fig 9.7

Loading ≠ unloading; the lower unloading force is the one that acts on the tooth.

Change force by re-tying Fig 9.8

A-NiTi force can be lowered simply by releasing and re-tying the wire.

Strength · stiffness · range Fig 9.10

Steel strongest & stiffest; M-NiTi least stiff but most range; β-Ti in between.

Diameter power law Fig 9.12

Double the diameter → strength ×8, stiffness ×16, range ÷2.

Beam length / attachment Fig 9.13

A longer span is far less stiff and has much more range.

Aligner stress-relaxation Fig 9.17

Thermoplastics lose 60–95% of their force over ~15 days.

NiTi behavior

NiTi sub-types
★ M-NiTi (martensitic / Nitinol)Naval Ordnance Lab; shape-memory, stabilized; low stiffness (0.17)
★ A-NiTi (austenitic / superelastic)Stress-induced transformation → constant-force plateau
Copper-NiTiTemperature-activated variant (force rises at mouth temperature)
Key behaviors
★ SuperelasticityFlat plateau = near-constant light force over a wide deflection
★ Shape memory / thermoelasticityRecovers a programmed shape on warming (M-NiTi)
★ HysteresisUnloading force < loading force — unloading is the clinically active one
Activation-dependent unloadingA-NiTi unloading stiffness varies with how far it was activated

Geometry: size & length power laws

The governing identity
★ Strength= Stiffness × Range
Springiness= 1 / stiffness
Diameter ↑ 2× (round wire)
★ Strength× 8 (∝ d³)
★ Stiffness× 16 (∝ d⁴)
★ Range÷ 2 (∝ 1/d)
Length ↑ 2× (cantilever beam)
★ Strength÷ 2 (∝ 1/L)
★ Stiffness÷ 8 (∝ 1/L³)
★ Range× 4 (∝ L²)
Other geometry
Supported both ends vs cantilevermuch stiffer & stronger, less range
Multistrand / coaxiallower stiffness & more range than a solid wire of the same size

Wire-property definitions

★ StrengthMaximum load the wire can deliver before permanent deformation (= stiffness × range).
★ StiffnessForce per unit deflection — the slope of the load-deflection curve.
★ RangeHow far the wire can be deflected and still spring back (working range).
SpringbackElastic recovery after deflection beyond the yield point.
ResilienceEnergy stored — area under the stress-strain curve up to yield.
★ FormabilityHow much permanent bending the wire takes before fracturing.
★ Modulus of elasticity (E)Slope of the stress-strain curve; stiffness is proportional to it.

Brackets, bonding & ligation

Bracket materials
★ Stainless steelStandard; strong, low friction, reasonable cost
TitaniumNickel-free option for Ni-allergic patients
★ Ceramic (alumina)Esthetic; mono- vs poly-crystalline; brittle, ↑ friction, enamel-damage risk on debond
Plastic / polycarbonateEsthetic but stains, creeps; often metal-/ceramic-slot reinforced
Bonding
★ Acid etch37% phosphoric acid, ~15–30 s → micromechanical retention
AdhesiveComposite resin; RMGIC releases fluoride; self-etch primers simplify steps
Ligation
★ Elastomeric moduleCheap, fast; adds friction and degrades/discolors
Steel ligature tieSecure, low force decay
★ Self-ligatingBuilt-in clip (passive/active); less friction, fewer visits claimed

Aligner polymers

★ ThermoplasticsPET-G (Duran), polyurethane (TPU), multilayer sheets.
Thickness≈ 0.75–1.0 mm sheet thermoformed to the model.
★ Stress-relaxation / creepLose 60–95% of force over ~15 days → staged tray changes.
Force deliveryIntermittent (removed for eating); attachments add control.
